Selective Outrage, Normalised Abuse

We're quick to raise alarm about how Gen Z speaks to each other online, but slower to notice the abuse we've normalised among ourselves as adults. If we want young people to argue with dignity, we have to first ask what they're watching us do.

Political discourse across the spectrum has become a masterclass in personal attack over argument. Opposition leaders get reduced to nicknames and mockery instead of engaged on policy. Ruling party leaders get called authoritarian or worse instead of challenged on governance. Their respective supporters — whichever side — pile on with the same contempt, dressed up as wit. None of it is debate. All of it is being watched by someone's kid.

The same pattern plays out with content creators. Across the political and religious spectrum, plenty of creators have built audiences by mocking what other people hold sacred — whether that's a religious tradition, a political figure, or a community's identity — because outrage drives views and shares better than nuance does. We reward it with our attention regardless of which side it's aimed at, then act surprised that public discourse has gotten cruder.

When people can't win an argument, many reach for a personal attack instead. Kids notice. They learn from what surrounds them, not just what they're told.

None of this means dissent, satire, or hard criticism should be off the table — a healthy society needs all three, aimed in every direction, including at power and at ideas people hold sacred. The line isn't disagreement, it's dehumanization. Debating a policy, a leader's record, or even a belief system is legitimate. Reducing a person to a slur, or treating cruelty as clever, is not — no matter who's doing it or who it's aimed at.

If we want the next generation to disagree without dehumanizing, someone has to show them what that looks like first. That starts at home, and it starts with holding our own side to the same standard we demand of the other.

By Preeta Sanjith
comment: A useful test is whether we apply the same standards to private conversations as public debates. Culture is shaped less by what we condemn publicly and more by what we tolerate daily.
